deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler, 'Tractatus de numerorum doctrina' (E792, written c. 1750, printed posthumously 1849), Ch. 10 on quadratic residues, §§363-369. On the previous page (§§345-362) Euler stated, without proof, rules for when n or -n is a quadratic residue of a prime of the form 4nq ± d·i². This page generalises those rules, restates the 'half of the classes mod 4n' principle, and proves the two easiest special cases.

§363. Suppose d and e each divide some number a^2 - n b^2. Then, for every prime P ≡ ±d·e·i^2 (mod 4n) with i odd, n is a quadratic residue of P, i.e. P divides some x^2 - n c^2. Euler says this follows from §§359-362 once one shows a composition lemma. The lemma: if d | a^2 - n b^2 and e | f^2 - n g^2, then de | h^2 - n k^2 for some h, k. He suggests this will follow by studying residues of squares modulo composite numbers. He does not prove it.

§364. Let D be any prime divisor of x^2 - n a^2 (the implicit setting is n not a perfect square and D not dividing 4n). Then D ≡ α (mod 4n), where α runs over exactly half of the φ(4n) classes coprime to 4n. The other half is excluded entirely. In modern terms, whether (n/D) = 1 depends only on D mod 4n, and the admissible classes form a subgroup of index 2.

§365. The same holds for prime divisors of x^2 + n a^2, i.e. for the residue -n. In both cases every odd square i^2 is an admissible α. If α is admissible, so is α·i^2. That is, the admissible set contains the squares and is closed under multiplication by squares.

§366 (proof for residue p, prime P = 4p+1). Since P ≡ 1 (mod 4), there exist a, b with P | a^2 + b^2, and b may be chosen freely. Subtract (4p+1)b^2 to get P | a^2 - 4p b^2. So 4p b^2 is a square residue mod P. Dividing by the square (2b)^2 shows p is a residue, i.e. P | a'^2 - p b'^2.
[Mine: equivalently 4p ≡ -1 (mod P), so p ≡ -1/4, and p is a residue because -1 is.]

§367 (residue -p). Take P | a^2 - b^2 (trivially, a = b). Adding (4p+1)b^2 gives P | a^2 + 4p b^2. So -4p b^2, and hence -p, is a residue. Euler writes the conclusion as 'aa+pbb', i.e. after removing the square factor 4.
[Mine: -p ≡ 1/4 (mod P), which is visibly a square.] Euler remarks that both ±p are residues of 4p+1.

§368 (prime P = 4f^2 p + i^2, i odd). Here P ≡ 1 (mod 4), so P | a^2 + b^2 is possible; also P | a^2 - b^2 trivially. Multiply both by i^2.
- From i^2 a^2 + i^2 b^2, subtract (4f^2 p + i^2) b^2 to get P | i^2 a^2 - 4f^2 p b^2.
- To i^2 a^2 - i^2 b^2, add (4f^2 p + i^2) b^2 to get P | i^2 a^2 + 4f^2 p b^2.
So ±4f^2 p b^2 are residues, hence ±p are residues. Thus P divides numbers of both forms x^2 + p y^2 and x^2 - p y^2.

Marginal note (*): The + case is obvious, since x = i, y = 2f gives x^2 + p y^2 = P itself.
Numerical examples with p = 2:
- 41 = 4·2^2·2 + 3^2. The pairs (x, y) = (7,2), (10,3), (13,8), (14,4), (17,1) give x^2 - 2y^2 = 41, 82, 41, 164, 287, all divisible by 41.
- 17 = 4·1·2 + 3^2. For y = 2, 1, 4, 3, 5 the paired x-values (x, 17 - x) are (12,5), (11,6), (10,7), (16,1), and printed '17,4'. The last should be (13,4).

§369. Summary, granting the conjectured observations. If the prime lies in one of the classes 4rq + 1, 4rq + α, 4rq + β, ... (half of the reduced classes mod 4r), then r is a quadratic residue. Analogous classes describe the residue -r. These coincide with the classes for +r when the divisor is ≡ 1 (mod 4) and are complementary when it is ≡ 3 (mod 4).
[Mine: this is (-r/P) = (-1/P)(r/P).]
errors: Footnote example for 17: the last pair is printed 'x = 17, 4' with y = 5. 17^2 - 2·25 = 239 is not divisible by 17. The correct pair is x = 13, 4 (169 - 50 = 119 = 7·17; 16 - 50 = -34). Every other pair sums to 17, so '17' is a slip (Euler's or the printer's) for 13.

§364-365 omit necessary hypotheses: n must not be a perfect square (otherwise every prime has n as a residue and there is no half-split), and the prime divisor must not divide 4n (and must be coprime to a, b).

§363 is only asserted. The composition lemma (de divides some h^2 - n k^2) needs coprimality conditions and is not proved here. The underlying claim is the conjectural general reciprocity statement, unproved by Euler.
§367: the derivation actually yields a^2 + 4p b^2, not a^2 + p b^2; the passage to a^2 + p b^2 (dividing out the square 4) is left implicit, as in §366. This is harmless.

results.what: For a non-square n, whether n (resp. -n) is a quadratic residue of a prime P depends only on P mod 4n. Exactly half of the reduced classes are admissible; they contain the squares and are closed under multiplication by squares. The classes for -r agree with those for r when P ≡ 1 (mod 4) and are complementary when P ≡ 3 (mod 4).
results.modern_name: Euler's formulation of the law of quadratic reciprocity (residue character of n depends on P mod 4n; kernel of a quadratic character mod 4n)
results.usually_credited_to: Conjectured by Euler (E164, 1744/1751; E552, 1783); proved by Gauss 1796/1801 (Legendre partial, 1785)

results.what: If d | a^2 - n b^2 and e | f^2 - n g^2, then de divides some h^2 - n k^2; consequently n is a residue of every prime ≡ ±de i^2 (mod 4n).
results.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the Jacobi/Kronecker symbol, composition of represented values / divisors of binary quadratic forms
results.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Euler and Lagrange; Jacobi symbol 1837

results.what: For a prime P = 4p + 1, both p and -p are quadratic residues mod P.
results.modern_name: Elementary consequence of the first supplementary law ((-1/P) = 1 for P ≡ 1 mod 4)

results.what: For a prime P = 4f^2 p + i^2 with i odd, both ±p are residues mod P; P divides numbers of both forms x^2 + p y^2 and x^2 - p y^2.
results.modern_name: Special case of quadratic reciprocity provable from (-1/P) = 1

deep.surprise_reason: Euler's empirical statement of quadratic reciprocity in the 'half of the classes mod 4n' form, and its appearance in the Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, are well documented (Weil, Lemmermeyer, Edwards). The proofs given here are easy special cases derived from -1 being a residue of primes ≡ 1 mod 4. Nothing on the page goes beyond what is known as Euler's.

checkable.sympy: all(sympy.legendre_symbol(p % (4*p+1), 4*p+1) == 1 and sympy.legendre_symbol((-p) % (4*p+1), 4*p+1) == 1 for p in range(1, 500) if sympy.isprime(4*p+1))
checkable.asserts: §366-367: for every prime P = 4p+1, both p and -p are quadratic residues mod P.

checkable.sympy: all(sympy.legendre_symbol(p % P, P) == 1 and sympy.legendre_symbol((-p) % P, P) == 1 for p in range(1, 30) for f in range(1, 6) for i in range(1, 20, 2) for P in [4*f**2*p + i**2] if sympy.isprime(P) and P % p != 0)
checkable.asserts: §368: for every prime P = 4 f^2 p + i^2 with i odd (and P not dividing p), ±p are quadratic residues mod P.
Footnote: the listed pairs make x^2 - 2y^2 divisible by 41.
Footnote: the pairs for 17 work, with the printed (17,5) corrected to (13,5).
The printed pair x = 17, y = 5 fails; it is a slip.

checkable.sympy: all(len({P % 12 for P in sympy.primerange(5, 3000) if sympy.legendre_symbol(3, P) == 1}) == 2 for _ in [0])
checkable.asserts: §364 for n = 3: the primes having 3 as a residue occupy exactly half (2 of 4) of the reduced classes mod 12, namely 1 and 11.

checkable.sympy: all(sympy.legendre_symbol(n % P, P) == sympy.legendre_symbol(n % Q, Q) for n in [2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10] for P in sympy.primerange(3, 600) for Q in sympy.primerange(3, 600) if P % (4*n) == Q % (4*n) and sympy.gcd(P, 4*n) == 1)
checkable.asserts: §364: (n/P) depends only on P mod 4n (Euler's form of reciprocity), checked for small n.

checkable.sympy: all(sympy.legendre_symbol((-r) % P, P) == (1 if P % 4 == 1 else -1) * sympy.legendre_symbol(r % P, P) for r in [2, 3, 5, 6, 7] for P in sympy.primerange(3, 1000) if r % P != 0)
checkable.asserts: §369: the classes for -r agree with those for r when P ≡ 1 mod 4 and are complementary when P ≡ 3 mod 4.

§367: the source reads 'aa+pbb', although the computation gives aa+4pbb. This is faithful to the image; no transcription change is needed.
